# **Learning Objectives** {.unnumbered}

By the end of this notebook you will be able to:

1.  Explain how decision trees choose splits using Gini impurity (classification) and RSS (regression), and why a single deep tree overfits
2.  Interpret a fitted decision tree visually and extract business rules
3.  Explain how random forests improve on single trees through bagging and feature randomness, and interpret variable importance plots
4.  Understand the sequential correction logic of boosted trees and explain the role of `learn_rate`, `tree_depth`, and `trees`
5.  Apply `step_unknown()` and `one_hot = TRUE` in a tree-appropriate recipe
6.  Compare all three methods against a Lasso logistic regression baseline using cross-validated metrics

> **Textbook references:** ISLR Chapter 8 (*Tree-Based Methods* — conceptual depth on trees, bagging, random forests, boosting); TMWR Chapter 12 (*Model Tuning and the Dangers of Overfitting* — tuning workflow applied to tree hyperparameters); TMWR Chapter 13 (*Ensemble Learning* — bagging, random forests, boosting); TMWR Chapter 18 (*Variable Importance and Partial Dependence Plots* — interpretation of tree-based models).

# **The Digital Campaign Dataset** {.unnumbered}

## Data Generation

We use a synthetic digital marketing campaign dataset with 4,000 customers. Two outcome variables serve as prediction targets throughout this module:

- **`purchased`** (yes/no) — whether the customer converted during the campaign period → **classification**
- **`avg_order_amt`** (\$) — the customer's average order value → **regression**

```{r create-data}
set.seed(6540)
n <- 4000

campaign_data <- tibble(
  customer_id = paste0("C", str_pad(1:n, 5, pad = "0")),
  age = round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, mean = 42, sd = 12), 18), 80)),
  income = round(rlnorm(n, meanlog = log(65000), sdlog = 0.55)),
  recency_days = round(pmin(rexp(n, rate = 1 / 45), 365)),
  freq_12mo = rpois(n, lambda = 3),
  site_visits_30d = rpois(n, lambda = 3),
  email_clicks_30d = rpois(n, lambda = 1.2),
  discount_rate_seen = sample(
    c(0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25),
    n,
    replace = TRUE,
    prob = c(0.20, 0.15, 0.20, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10)
  ),
  channel = sample(
    c("email", "paid_search", "social", "direct", "display"),
    n,
    replace = TRUE,
    prob = c(0.35, 0.22, 0.18, 0.15, 0.10)
  ),
  region = sample(
    c("West", "South", "Midwest", "Northeast"),
    n,
    replace = TRUE
  ),
  loyalty_tier = factor(
    sample(
      c("Bronze", "Silver", "Gold", "Platinum"),
      n,
      replace = TRUE,
      prob = c(0.45, 0.30, 0.18, 0.07)
    ),
    levels = c("Bronze", "Silver", "Gold", "Platinum"),
    ordered = TRUE
  ),
  device = sample(
    c("mobile", "desktop", "tablet"),
    n,
    replace = TRUE,
    prob = c(0.58, 0.34, 0.08)
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    # cart_adds: derived from engagement variables
    cart_adds_30d = rbinom(
      n,
      size = 5,
      prob = pmin(
        0.04 + 0.025 * site_visits_30d + 0.06 * email_clicks_30d,
        0.70
      )
    ),

    # avg_order_amt: basket size driven by income, loyalty, channel,
    # device, discount, and a nonlinear discount × loyalty interaction
    # (trees will discover this interaction automatically)
    avg_order_amt = round(
      rlnorm(
        n,
        meanlog = log(65) +
          0.12 * log(income / 65000) + # income effect (modest)
          case_when(
            # loyalty tier effect
            loyalty_tier == "Platinum" ~ 0.45,
            loyalty_tier == "Gold" ~ 0.28,
            loyalty_tier == "Silver" ~ 0.12,
            TRUE ~ 0
          ) +
          case_when(
            # channel effect
            channel == "email" ~ 0.18,
            channel == "direct" ~ 0.14,
            channel == "paid_search" ~ 0.05,
            channel == "social" ~ -0.08,
            channel == "display" ~ -0.18,
            TRUE ~ 0
          ) +
          case_when(
            # device effect
            device == "desktop" ~ 0.15,
            device == "tablet" ~ 0.02,
            device == "mobile" ~ -0.12,
            TRUE ~ 0
          ) +
          0.12 * discount_rate_seen + # discount boosts basket
          # interaction: discounts matter MORE for price-sensitive Bronze customers
          if_else(loyalty_tier == "Bronze", 0.35 * discount_rate_seen, 0) +
          0.08 * cart_adds_30d + # more cart adds → bigger basket
          0.04 * freq_12mo, # frequent buyers → larger orders
        sdlog = 0.38
      ),
      2
    ),

    # purchased: binary classification outcome
    # driven by engagement, RFM, loyalty, channel, and nonlinear interactions
    # hidden data-generating process — in real life we would not know this
    purchased = {
      loyalty_effect <- case_when(
        loyalty_tier == "Bronze" ~ 0,
        loyalty_tier == "Silver" ~ 0.55, # bumped from 0.40 for ordering
        loyalty_tier == "Gold" ~ 0.90,
        loyalty_tier == "Platinum" ~ 1.25
      )
      channel_effect <- case_when(
        channel == "email" ~ 0.45,
        channel == "paid_search" ~ 0.18,
        channel == "social" ~ 0.12,
        channel == "direct" ~ 0.30,
        channel == "display" ~ -0.22
      )
      device_effect <- case_when(
        device == "mobile" ~ 0.10,
        device == "desktop" ~ 0.25,
        device == "tablet" ~ -0.08
      )
      # nonlinear interactions — trees discover these; linear models miss them
      discount_bronze_boost <- if_else(
        discount_rate_seen >= 0.15 & loyalty_tier == "Bronze",
        1.10,
        0
      )
      high_engagement_boost <- if_else(
        site_visits_30d >= 5 & email_clicks_30d >= 2,
        1.15,
        0
      )
      recent_frequent_boost <- if_else(
        recency_days < 20 & freq_12mo >= 4,
        0.80,
        0
      )
      email_click_boost <- if_else(
        channel == "email" & email_clicks_30d >= 2,
        0.60,
        0
      )

      logit_purchase <- -5.0 + # intercept → ~ 1/(1 + exp(-(-5)) = 0.67% base rate; predictors raise overall purchase rate to around 24%
        0.70 * log1p(site_visits_30d) +
        0.55 * log1p(email_clicks_30d) +
        0.75 * cart_adds_30d +
        0.35 * freq_12mo -
        0.022 * recency_days +
        0.30 * log(income / 65000) +
        loyalty_effect +
        channel_effect +
        device_effect +
        discount_bronze_boost +
        high_engagement_boost +
        recent_frequent_boost +
        email_click_boost +
        rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.45)

      factor(
        rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = plogis(logit_purchase)),
        levels = c(1, 0),
        labels = c("yes", "no")
      )
    },

    # 7% missingness in income; 5% in avg_order_amt (MAR)
    income = if_else(runif(n) < 0.07, NA_real_, income),
    avg_order_amt = if_else(runif(n) < 0.05, NA_real_, avg_order_amt)
  ) |>
  select(
    customer_id,
    age,
    income,
    recency_days,
    freq_12mo,
    avg_order_amt,
    site_visits_30d,
    email_clicks_30d,
    discount_rate_seen,
    cart_adds_30d,
    channel,
    region,
    loyalty_tier,
    device,
    purchased
  )

glimpse(campaign_data)
```

## Technical Note on Data Generation

### Braces in `mutate()` = 1. Temporary effect variables

In `mutate()`, this syntax:

``` r
purchased = {
  ...
}
```

means:

> “Run all the code inside the braces, and use the value of the final expression as the new purchased column.”

The braces { } create a **code block**. They let you write several intermediate steps when defining one variable.

In the campaign data :

```{r}
#| eval: false
purchased <- {
  loyalty_effect <- ...
  channel_effect <- ...
  device_effect <- ...

  discount_bronze_boost <- ...
  high_engagement_boost <- ...

  logit_purchase <- ...

  factor(
    rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = plogis(logit_purchase)),
    levels = c(1, 0),
    labels = c("yes", "no")
  )
}
```

The important rule is that **the last expression is returned.**

Therefore, that factor vector becomes the purchased column.

The temporary variables such as `loyalty_effect`, `channel_effect`, `logit_purchase` are used to calculate the result, but they do not become columns in `campaign_data`.

> Without braces, you would need either one very long expression or would need to create several temporary columns in the dataset. The braces make the code easier to organize while preventing all those helper variables from appearing in the final tibble.

> The braces is not a special mutate() operator but a general R code block. `mutate()` simply accepts the value returned by that block.

### Loyalty-tier effect

``` r
loyalty_effect <- case_when(
  loyalty_tier == "Bronze" ~ 0,
  loyalty_tier == "Silver" ~ 0.55,
  loyalty_tier == "Gold" ~ 0.90,
  loyalty_tier == "Platinum" ~ 1.25
)
```

Each customer receives an adjustment based on loyalty tier:

| Loyalty tier | Logit adjustment |
|--------------|------------------|
| Bronze       | 0.00             |
| Silver       | 0.55             |
| Gold         | 0.90             |
| Platinum     | 1.25             |

- Bronze is the reference group. Higher loyalty tiers receive increasingly positive adjustments, making purchase more likely.

- These numbers are measured on the **log-odds scale**, not directly as percentage-point increases.

- For example, Platinum’s coefficient of `1.25` multiplies the odds of purchase by:

  $e^{1.25} \approx 3.49$

- Holding everything else constant, a Platinum customer has about **3.5 times** the purchase odds of an otherwise similar Bronze customer.

### `logit_purchase`

```{r}
#| eval: false
logit_purchase <- -5.0 + # intercept → ~ 1/(1 + exp(-(-5)) = 0.67% base rate; predictors raise overall purchase rate to around 24%
  0.70 * log1p(site_visits_30d) +
  0.55 * log1p(email_clicks_30d) +
  0.75 * cart_adds_30d +
  0.35 * freq_12mo -
  0.022 * recency_days +
  0.30 * log(income / 65000) +
  loyalty_effect +
  channel_effect +
  device_effect +
  discount_bronze_boost +
  high_engagement_boost +
  recent_frequent_boost +
  email_click_boost +
  rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.45)

factor(
  rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = plogis(logit_purchase)),
  levels = c(1, 0),
  labels = c("yes", "no")
)
```

- **Intercept** = Baseline probability by converting the logit score to purchase probability as:

$$P(\text{purchased} = \text{yes}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(-5)}} 
                   = \frac{1}{1 + e^{5}} \approx 0.0067 \approx 0.67\%$$

- The dataset may end up with a purchase rate around **24%** after the engagement, loyalty, frequency, channel, interaction, and random effects are added.

- `log1p(x)` = `log(1 + x)` is used to reduce the impact of extreme values in `site_visits_30d` and `email_clicks_30d`.

- **`plogis()`** is used to convert the logit score to a probability between 0 and 1.

$$P_i = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\eta_i}}$$
where $\eta_i$ is `logit_purchase`.

For example:

| `logit_purchase` | Purchase probability |
|------------------|----------------------|
| −5               | 0.7%                 |
| −3               | 4.7%                 |
| −2               | 11.9%                |
| −1               | 26.9%                |
| 0                | 50.0%                |
| 1                | 73.1%                |
| 2                | 88.1%                |
| 3                | 95.3%                |

A higher logit means a higher probability, but the relationship is nonlinear.

- `rbinom():`**Binominal Distribution**

The general binomial model is:

$$X ∼ Binomial⁡(m,p)$$
where:

- X is the number of successes
- m is the number of opportunities or trials
- p is the probability of success on each trial

**Example:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
# rbinom(n, size, prob)
rbinom(10, 5, 0.6)
```

**Campaign Data:**

In the code, `size = 5` means:

- Each customer is given five possible opportunities to add an item to the cart.

For each customer, `rbinom()` returns an integer from 0 through 5:

### `cart_adds_30d`

``` r
# cart_adds: derived from engagement variables
    cart_adds_30d = rbinom(
      n,
      size = 5,
      prob = pmin(
        0.04 + 0.025 * site_visits_30d + 0.06 * email_clicks_30d,
        0.70
      )
```

> Note that unlike the simple example above where every customer has the same prob = 0.6, in the campaign data each customer's cart-add probability is different — it depends on their engagement level (`site_visits_30d` and `email_clicks_30d`), capped at 0.70. More engaged customers have higher cart-add rates, which in turn predicts higher purchase probability.

- A customer with `site_visits_30d` = 0 and `email_clicks_30d` = 0 has a probability of only 0.04 (almost never adds to cart), while a highly engaged customer can reach the cap of 0.70.

## Outcome Variable Description

### `purchased` — Classification Outcome

`purchased` reflects a realistic digital marketing conversion funnel with **four layers of signal**:

::: {.callout-note title="What drives purchase probability"}
**Behavioral engagement (strongest signals)**

- `cart_adds_30d` — customers who add items to their cart are most likely to convert; this is the single strongest predictor
- `email_clicks_30d` and `site_visits_30d` — active engagement in the 30 days before the campaign predicts conversion

**RFM signals**

- `freq_12mo` — frequent past buyers are more likely to convert again
- `recency_days` — customers who purchased more recently are more responsive

**Customer value signals**

- `loyalty_tier` — Platinum \> Gold \> Silver \> Bronze conversion rates
- `income` — modest positive effect

**Campaign exposure signals**

- `channel` — email and direct channels convert best; display converts worst
- `discount_rate_seen` — higher discounts boost conversion, especially for Bronze tier customers (nonlinear interaction)
- `device` — desktop users convert at slightly higher rates than mobile

**Nonlinear interactions (trees find these; linear models miss them)**

- High discount × Bronze tier → extra conversion boost (price-sensitive customers)
- High site visits AND email clicks → disproportionate engagement effect
- Recently active AND frequent buyers → amplified recency × frequency boost
- Email channel AND multiple email clicks → channel × engagement amplification
:::

```{r response-rate}
campaign_data |>
  count(purchased) |>
  mutate(rate = round(n / sum(n), 3)) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Overall Purchase Rate")
```

```{r purchase-by-segment}
# Purchase rate by loyalty tier and channel
p1 <- campaign_data |>
  group_by(loyalty_tier) |>
  summarise(rate = mean(purchased == "yes")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = loyalty_tier, y = rate, fill = loyalty_tier)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("#9e9e9e", "#C0A060", "#B0B0B0", "#4A90D9")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Purchase Rate by Loyalty Tier", x = NULL, y = "Purchase rate") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p2 <- campaign_data |>
  group_by(channel) |>
  summarise(rate = mean(purchased == "yes")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(channel, rate), y = rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#154734", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Purchase Rate by Channel", x = NULL, y = "Purchase rate") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p1 + p2
```

### `avg_order_amt` — Regression Outcome

`avg_order_amt` reflects how basket size varies with customer characteristics and campaign context:

::: {.callout-note title="What drives average order value"}
**Income** (moderate, r ≈ 0.14): higher-income customers tend to buy more expensive items or fill larger baskets.

**Loyalty tier** (clear gradient): Platinum members shop across more categories and are less price-constrained than Bronze members.

- Bronze ≈ \$96 \| Silver ≈ \$104 \| Gold ≈ \$119 \| Platinum ≈ \$144

**Channel** (directional): email and direct traffic drives deliberate, larger purchases; social and display drive impulse buys with smaller baskets.

- Email ≈ \$119 \| Direct ≈ \$111 \| Social ≈ \$90 \| Display ≈ \$83

**Device** (meaningful): desktop users complete larger, more intentional purchases; mobile skews toward smaller, faster transactions.

- Desktop ≈ \$125 \| Tablet ≈ \$105 \| Mobile ≈ \$94

**Cart adds** (strongest behavioral signal, r ≈ 0.15): customers who added more items to their cart predictably complete larger orders.

**Nonlinear interaction**: high discounts increase basket size more for Bronze customers (price-sensitive) than for Platinum (already committed). Trees will find this interaction; linear regression will need it explicitly.
:::

```{r order-amt-eda}
p3 <- ggplot(campaign_data, aes(x = avg_order_amt)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#154734", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Average Order Amount",
    x = "Average order amount ($)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p4 <- campaign_data |>
  filter(!is.na(avg_order_amt)) |>
  group_by(loyalty_tier) |>
  summarise(mean_order = mean(avg_order_amt)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = loyalty_tier, y = mean_order, fill = loyalty_tier)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("#9e9e9e", "#C0A060", "#B0B0B0", "#4A90D9")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean Order Amount by Loyalty Tier",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Mean order amount ($)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p3 + p4
```

# Part 1: Trees {.unnumbered style="font-size: 28pt; font-weight: bold; color: #f1861b;"}

# **Train/Test Splits, Recipes, CV Folds**

> Data splits, recipes, and CV folds will be used across all methods.

## Splits

```{r split}
set.seed(617)
camp_split <- initial_split(campaign_data, prop = 0.80, strata = purchased)
camp_train <- training(camp_split)
camp_test <- testing(camp_split)

cat("Training rows:", nrow(camp_train), "\n")
cat("Test rows    :", nrow(camp_test), "\n")
cat(
  "Purchase rate (train):",
  round(mean(camp_train$purchased == "yes"), 3),
  "\n"
)
cat(
  "Purchase rate (test) :",
  round(mean(camp_test$purchased == "yes"), 3),
  "\n"
)
```

## Recipes

### Why Trees Need a Different Recipe

> Tree-based models have fundamentally different preprocessing requirements than linear models like Lasso logistic regression.

::: {.callout-note title="What trees DON'T need — and why"}
- **`step_normalize()`** — Trees split on *rank order*, not *magnitude*. A split at "income \> 60,000" produces identical results whether income is on the dollar scale or the normalized (z-score) scale. **Normalization adds no value** and just makes coefficient interpretation harder.

- **`step_log()` on predictors** — Logarithm is a monotone transformation — it preserves rank order. If the optimal split for `income` in dollar scale is at \$60,000, the optimal split in log scale is at log(\$60,000). The tree finds the same split either way. **No need to transform predictors**.

- **Consequence**: the recipe for trees is simpler and produces more interpretable split values (dollar amounts, raw counts) in the tree output.
:::

To avoid potential problems with step_log() in recipe, we will add log-transformed variable `log_avg_order_amt` to the data - train set and test set.

```{r log-transform}
# log-transform the OUTCOME (not predictors) to handle right skew

camp_train <- camp_train |>
  mutate(log_avg_order_amt = log(avg_order_amt))
```

### Classification Recipe

```{r class-recipe}
# Classification recipe — simpler than Module 2's Lasso recipe
class_rec <- recipe(
  purchased ~ .,
  data = camp_train
) |>
  update_role(customer_id, new_role = "ID") |>
  update_role(log_avg_order_amt, new_role = "unused") |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) |> # handle previously unseen levels
  step_unknown(all_nominal_predictors()) |> # handle missing categorical values
  step_zv(all_predictors())

class_rec
```

::: {.callout-note title="Two new recipe steps for tree models"}
- **`step_unknown()`** — In production, new data may contain factor levels not seen during training (e.g., a new marketing channel is launched after the model was built). Without handling, this causes a prediction error. `step_unknown()` explicitly encodes unseen levels as a new "unknown" category rather than crashing. This is a production-readiness step that becomes important when models are deployed.

- **`one_hot = TRUE` in `step_dummy()`** — Standard dummy encoding creates $k - 1$ columns per factor (dropping one reference level) to avoid multicollinearity in linear models. Trees have no multicollinearity problem — they can split on any column independently.

  - Using `one_hot = TRUE` creates all $k$ columns, which sometimes helps trees find better splits by having each category available as a direct split candidate.

  - For example, with `one_hot = TRUE` the tree can split directly on `channel_email == 1` rather than inferring the email effect from the remaining categories.
:::

### Regression Recipe

```{r reg-recipe}
# Regression recipe: predict avg_order_amt

reg_rec <- recipe(
  log_avg_order_amt ~ .,
  data = camp_train
) |>
  update_role(customer_id, new_role = "ID") |>
  update_role(purchased, new_role = "unused") |>
  update_role(avg_order_amt, new_role = "outcome_original") |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) |> # handle previously unseen levels
  step_unknown(all_nominal_predictors()) |> # handle missing categorical value
  step_zv(all_predictors())

reg_rec
```

::: {.callout-note title="Why log-transform the outcome but not the predictors?"}
- `avg_order_amt` is right-skewed — a few very large orders pull the distribution out. For regression trees, the split criterion is **RSS (Residual Sum of Squares)**: the algorithm finds the split that minimizes the total squared deviation from the group mean within each node.

- Squared errors punish large outliers heavily — a single \$500 order can disproportionately influence which split is chosen. Log-transforming the outcome compresses the scale, reducing the leverage of outliers on split decisions and producing a more balanced tree.

**Note** that predictions will be on the log scale — you need to **`exp()`** them to get back to dollar amounts.

- We do **not** log-transform the predictors because (as explained above) trees are rank-order invariant — monotone predictor transforms have no effect on splits.
:::

## Cross-Validation Folds

```{r cv-folds}
set.seed(2025)
camp_folds <- vfold_cv(camp_train, v = 10, strata = purchased)
camp_folds
```

# **Decision Trees**

A decision tree is a **non-parametric model** that recursively partitions the predictor space into a set of rectangular, non-overlapping regions. For any new observation, the tree traces a path from top to bottom through a series of binary (yes/no) split questions (e.g., *"Is `cart_adds_30d`* $\ge 2$?") until it lands in a final region, where it assigns a prediction.

## Conceptual Background

### Key Terminology

- **Root Node:** The topmost node in the tree representing the entire dataset before any splits occur.
- **Internal (Decision) Node:** A node that splits into two child nodes based on a specific threshold of a single predictor variable.
- **Child Node / Parent Node:** When a node splits, the original node is the *parent*, and the resulting sub-nodes are the *children*.
- **Terminal Node (Leaf):** A final node at the bottom of the tree with no further splits. All observations falling into a leaf receive the same prediction:
  - **Classification:** The majority class (or class proportions) in that leaf.
  - **Regression:** The mean target value ($\bar{y}$) of training points in that leaf.
- **Splitting Rule:** The specific criterion (e.g., Gini impurity or RSS) used to determine the best variable and threshold for dividing data at a node.
- **Pruning:** The process of trimming back fully-grown branches to reduce model complexity and prevent overfitting.

### How Decision Trees Work

A decision tree recursively splits the training data into regions by asking a series of binary questions: "Is `cart_adds_30d` ≥ 2?" → yes/no, then "Is `recency_days` \< 30?" → yes/no, and so on.

#### A. Classification Trees (Gini Impurity)

Splits are selected to minimize the **Gini Impurity** ($G$) across the child nodes:

$$G = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat{p}_{mk}^2$$

Where $\hat{p}_{mk}$ is the proportion of training observations in node $m$ belonging to class $k$.

::: {.callout-note title="Interpreting Gini Impurity"}
- $G = 0$ (Completely Pure): Every customer in the node belongs to the exact same class.
- $G \approx 0.5$ (Maximum Impurity for 2 Classes): Class proportions are split evenly ($50/50$).
- The algorithm chooses the split that yields the largest **reduction in weighted Gini impurity** when comparing the parent node to its two child nodes.
:::

#### B. Regression Trees (Residual Sum of Squares)

For continuous outcomes, splits are selected to minimize the **Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)**:

$$\text{RSS} = \sum_{m=1}^{M} \sum_{i \in R_m} (y_i - \bar{y}_{R_m})^2$$

Where $\bar{y}_{R_m}$ is the average response value of training points in region $R_m$.

### Controlling Tree Complexity (Hyperparameters)

::: {.callout-warning title="Why a single deep tree overfits"}
- A fully grown tree will keep splitting until every leaf contains a single training observation — achieving 100% training accuracy but completely memorizing noise.
- This is the same overfitting problem we saw with KNN at k=1 in Module 5.
- The solution is **pruning**: limiting tree complexity via the `cost_complexity` (cp) hyperparameter, which adds a penalty for each additional leaf node.
:::

Unconstrained decision trees will continue splitting until every leaf is completely pure, leading to severe **overfitting** (high variance). In `tidymodels` (via the `rpart` engine), three key hyperparameters control tree growth:

1.  **Tree Depth (`tree_depth`):** The maximum length of any path from the root node to a leaf node.

2.  **Minimum Split Size (`min_n`):** The minimum number of training observations required in a node for a split to be attempted.

3.  **Cost-Complexity Parameter (`cost_complexity` /** $\alpha$): A penalty factor that penalizes larger trees. The algorithm minimizes:
    $$\text{Cost (or Tree Score)} = \text{Error} + \alpha \times (\text{Number of Leaves})$$

    - $\text{Cost}$ is Tree score.
    - $\text{Error}$ is SSR in Regression trees
    - The more the leaves, the greater the penalty
    - $\alpha$ is a tuning parameter, also called Cp.
      - $\alpha = 0$: We will get unpruned, full-size tree; complex tree.
      - Higher $\alpha$: Smaller, simpler tree with fewer leaves.

::: {.callout-tip title="Feature Scaling & Categorical Variables"}
Decision trees evaluate variables **one at a time** (monotonic splits), which gives them two major advantages:

- **No Scaling Required:** Decision trees are completely invariant to monotonic transformations. Normalizing or standardizing features (e.g., `step_normalize()`) does **not** change tree performance.

- **Missing Values & Outliers:** Trees naturally accommodate non-linear relationships and are robust to severe feature outliers.
:::

## Clasification Tree

### Fitting a Classification Tree

```{r tree-fit}
tree_spec <- decision_tree(
  cost_complexity = 0.001, # cp: penalty per leaf — smaller = deeper tree
  tree_depth = 10, # maximum depth allowed
  min_n = 20 # minimum observations per node to allow a split
) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

tree_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(class_rec) |>
  add_model(tree_spec)

tree_fit <- fit(tree_wf, data = camp_train)
```

### Visualizing the Tree

```{r tree-plot, fig.height=7, fig.width=12}
tree_fit |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot(
    type = 4,
    extra = 104, # show class probability + % of observations
    box.palette = "GnBu",
    shadow.col = "gray",
    nn = TRUE,
    main = "Decision Tree — Purchase Prediction"
  )
```

::: {.callout-note title="How to read the tree"}
Each node shows three numbers: the **predicted class** (yes/no), the **probability of "yes"**, and the **percentage of training observations** that reach that node.

- **Root node** (top): the starting point — all training data, predicting the majority class at the overall response rate
- **Internal nodes**: each shows the split condition (e.g., `cart_adds_30d < 2`); left branch = TRUE, right branch = FALSE
- **Leaf nodes** (bottom): terminal predictions — the class and probability assigned to any new customer who follows that path through the tree

The first few splits reveal the most important predictors — the algorithm chose them because they produce the largest Gini reduction.
:::

### Extracting the Fitted Tree

```{r}
tree_fit |>
  extract_fit_engine()
```

#### Node 1: The Root Node (The Starting Point)

``` r
1) root 3199 764 no (0.23882463 0.76117537)
```

- **`1) root`**: This is **Node 1**, the top of the tree representing the entire dataset before any splits occur.

- **`3199` (**$n$): There are **3,199 total observations** in this training set.

- **`764` (loss)**: If we predict the overall majority class for everyone at this step, we make **764 errors** (misclassifications).

- **`no` (`yval`)**: The majority prediction at this node is `"no"`.

- **`(0.23882463 0.76117537)` (`yprob`)**: The proportion of classes in this node:

  - Class 1 (e.g., `"yes"`): **23.88%** ($764 / 3,199 \approx 0.2388$)

  - Class 2 (e.g., `"no"`): **76.12%** ($3,199 - 764 = 2,435$ actual `"no"` cases; $2,435 / 3,199 \approx 0.7612$ ).

#### Node 2: The First Branch (Child Node)

``` r
2) cart_adds_30d>=1.5 789 355 no (0.44993663 0.55006337)
```

- **`2)`**: This is **Node 2**, the left child node created by answering "Yes" to the split condition.

- **`cart_adds_30d>=1.5`**: The decision rule that routed data into this node. (Customers who had **2 or more cart adds** in the last 30 days).

- **`789` (**$n$): Out of 3,199 customers, **789 met this condition**.

- **`355` (loss)**: Predicting `"no"` for everyone in this group leads to **355 misclassifications**.

- **`no` (`yval`)**: `"no"` remains the predicted majority class label for this node.

- **`(0.44993663 0.55006337)` (`yprob`)**: Notice how the distribution shifted significantly compared to the root node:

  - Class 1 (`"yes"`): Increased from **23.88%** $\rightarrow$ 44.99%

  - Class 2 (`"no"`): Decreased from **76.12%** $\rightarrow$ 55.01%

#### Executive Interpretation

> *"At the root level (3,199 total customers), about 76.1% of customers are class 'no'. The tree selects `cart_adds_30d` as its very first splitting variable. For customers with at least 2 cart additions (`cart_adds_30d >= 1.5`), the probability of being in class 'yes' nearly doubles from 23.9% to 45.0%."*

::: {.callout-tip title="How to Identify Sister Nodes"}
In `rpart` tree printouts, child nodes follow a binary numbering convention:

- Node $N$'s left child is $2N$ (e.g., Node 1 $\rightarrow$ **Node 2**).

- Node $N$'s right child is $2N + 1$ (e.g., Node 1 $\rightarrow$ **Node 3** for `cart_adds_30d < 1.5`).
:::

### Reading Business Rules from the Tree

```{r tree-rules}
# Extract rules from the tree as text
library(rpart.plot)
tree_fit |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot::rpart.rules(cover = TRUE, style = "tall")
```

#### How to Read a Single Rule Block

Every block in the output follows this exact template:

``` r
..y is [PREDICTION] with cover [SIZE OF SEGMENT] when
    [Condition 1]
    [Condition 2]
    [Condition 3]
```

- `y is ...`: The target outcome the tree is predicting (e.g., probability of purchasing). Higher numbers mean higher probability.

- `cover ...`: How large this segment is.

- `cover 31%` means 31% of all your data falls into this exact bucket.

- `cover 0%` means less than 0.5% (a tiny fraction) fell here.

- `when ...`: The exact behavior or demographics required to place a customer into this segment. All conditions in a block must be true at the same time.

::: callout-tip
#### Decision Tree Analysis: Key Drivers of Purchase Behavior

To identify the primary behavioral patterns driving customer conversion, an `rpart` decision tree model was evaluated across the dataset using the target variable `Purchased` (1 = Purchase, 0 = No Purchase).

**Segment A: Passive Recent Engagers (31% of all customers)**

``` r
..y is 0.93 with cover 31% when
    cart_adds_30d < 1.5
    recency_days >= 28
    email_clicks_30d < 1.5
```

- Purchase Likelihood: 93%
- Volume: 31% of your entire customer base
- *Interpretation*: This is your core conversion engine. Customers who haven't needed to add items to their cart recently or click marketing emails because they are already established, returning buyers.

**Segment B: Low-Threshold Browsers (11% of all customers)**

``` r
..y is 0.91 with cover 11% when
    cart_adds_30d < 1.5
    recency_days < 28
    freq_12mo < 3.5
    site_visits_30d < 3.5
    email_clicks_30d < 1.5
```

- Purchase Likelihood: 91%
- Volume: 11% of your customer base
- *Interpretation*: Recent visitors with lower overall engagement metrics who still convert at extremely high rates without needing heavy promotional pushing.

**Segment C: High Intent / High Friction (Cart Abandoners)**

``` r
..y is 0.08 with cover 1% when
    cart_adds_30d >= 1.5
    recency_days < 27
    site_visits_30d is 1.5 to 4.5
    email_clicks_30d >= 1.5
    channel_email >= 0.5
```

- Purchase Likelihood: Only 8% (92% non-conversion rate!)
- *Interpretation*: These users actively add items to their cart (cart_adds_30d \>= 1.5), visit the site, and click email links, yet fail to convert. This indicates high intent but potential friction at checkout (e.g., unexpected shipping costs or payment issues).
:::

### Classification Tree Performance

```{r test-set-log-transform}
# Add log_avg_order_amt to your test set
camp_test <- camp_test |>
  mutate(log_avg_order_amt = log(avg_order_amt))
```

```{r tree-metrics}
tree_preds <- augment(tree_fit, new_data = camp_test)

tree_preds |>
  metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc, sens, spec)(
    truth = purchased,
    estimate = .pred_class,
    .pred_yes
  )

# Confusion matrix
conf_mat(tree_preds, truth = purchased, estimate = .pred_class) |>
  autoplot(type = "heatmap")
```

### The Overfitting Problem — Shallow vs. Deep Tree

```{r tree-overfit}
# Compare a very deep tree vs. a pruned tree
fit_tree_cp <- function(cp_val) {
  spec <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = cp_val) |>
    set_engine("rpart") |>
    set_mode("classification")
  wf <- workflow() |> add_recipe(class_rec) |> add_model(spec)
  list(
    train = augment(fit(wf, data = camp_train), new_data = camp_train) |>
      roc_auc(truth = purchased, .pred_yes) |>
      mutate(cp = cp_val, data = "train"),
    test = augment(fit(wf, data = camp_train), new_data = camp_test) |>
      roc_auc(truth = purchased, .pred_yes) |>
      mutate(cp = cp_val, data = "test")
  )
}

cp_vals <- c(0.0001, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05)
overfit_results <- map(cp_vals, fit_tree_cp) |>
  map(bind_rows) |>
  bind_rows()

overfit_results |>
  select(cp, data, .estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = data, values_from = .estimate) |>
  mutate(gap = round(train - test, 4)) |>
  arrange(cp)
```

```{r tree-overfit-plot}
overfit_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log10(cp), y = .estimate, color = data, group = data)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(train = "#B08D57", test = "#154734")) +
  labs(
    title = "Decision Tree — Train vs. Test AUC Across Pruning Levels",
    subtitle = "Small cp = deep (complex) tree; large cp = shallow (pruned) tree",
    x = "log10(cost_complexity)",
    y = "ROC AUC",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Reading the overfitting plot"}
As `cost_complexity` decreases (left side of the x-axis), the tree grows deeper — training AUC climbs toward 1.0 as the tree memorizes the data. Test AUC *peaks at an intermediate complexity level* and then declines — the tree has started fitting noise that doesn't generalize.

The gap between training and test AUC is the **resubstitution gap** from Module 3. For trees, this gap can be enormous — a deep tree achieving near-100% training AUC is the most extreme overfitting case we've seen in this course.
:::

## Regression Tree

### How Regression Trees Work

While classification trees predict discrete categorical outcomes (e.g., `"yes"` vs. `"no"`), **regression trees** predict a **continuous numerical target variable** (e.g., `revenue`, `income`, or `num_orders`).

Instead of assigning a majority class label at a leaf node, a regression tree calculates the **average target value (**$\bar{y}$) of all training observations that fall into that specific terminal region:

$$\hat{y}_{R_m} = \bar{y}_{R_m} = \frac{1}{n_m} \sum_{i \in R_m} y_i$$

Where $n_m$ is the number of observations in leaf node region $R_m$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Splitting Criterion: Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)

Regression trees recursively partition the feature space by choosing splits that cause the largest reduction in **Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)**:

$$\text{RSS} = \sum_{m=1}^{M} \sum_{i \in R_m} (y_i - \bar{y}_{R_m})^2$$

At each node $m$, the algorithm searches across every available predictor $X_j$ and every possible split value $s$, selecting the pair $(X_j, s)$ that minimizes the combined RSS of the left child region ($R_1$) and right child region ($R_2$):

$$\text{RSS}_{\text{split}} = \sum_{i \in R_1(j,s)} (y_i - \bar{y}_{R_1})^2 + \sum_{i \in R_2(j,s)} (y_i - \bar{y}_{R_2})^2$$

::: {.callout-note title="Key Architectural Property: Step Functions"}
A regression tree does **not** fit a smooth, continuous line or curve through data like linear or polynomial regression does.

Instead, it fits a **piecewise constant surface** (a step function). Observations falling into the exact same terminal leaf node receive the exact same predicted value, regardless of where they lie within that feature region.
:::

### Regression Tree Pruning

#### The Need for Pruning

If left unconstrained, a decision tree will continue splitting data until every leaf node contains only a single observation (or a tiny cluster of points).

While a fully grown, complex tree achieves **near-zero training error** ($\text{RSS} \approx 0$), it severely overfits the training data by fitting to noise rather than signal. This results in **high variance** and poor generalization on unseen test data.

Rather than stopping tree growth early using arbitrary thresholds (which can miss valuable deeper splits), the standard strategy is to:

1.  **Grow a large, fully expanded tree** ($T_0$).
2.  **Prune it back** to obtain a smaller subtree that balances model complexity and predictive performance.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### Cost-Complexity Pruning (Weakest-Link Pruning)

The most widely used method for pruning regression trees is **Cost-Complexity Pruning** (also known as $C_p$ or Weakest-Link Pruning).

Instead of evaluating every possible subtree (which is computationally impossible for large trees), Cost-Complexity Pruning indexes a sequence of subtrees using a non-negative **tuning parameter** $\alpha$ (often written as $C_p$ in R).

For a given $\alpha$, the algorithm minimizes the following objective function:

$$\text{Cost Complexity} = \sum_{m=1}^{|T|} \text{RSS}_m + \alpha \cdot |T|$$

Where:

- $\text{RSS}_m$: The Residual Sum of Squares in leaf $m$.
- $|T|$: The total number of terminal leaf nodes in subtree $T$ (representing model complexity).
- $\alpha$ (or $C_p$): The **complexity parameter** that penalizes the tree for having too many leaves.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### How $\alpha$ ($C_p$) Controls Tree Size

- **When** $\alpha = 0$: There is no penalty for complexity. The algorithm selects the fully grown, unpruned tree ($T_0$).
- **As** $\alpha$ increases: Small branches that yield only minor reductions in RSS are penalized and "collapsed" back into parent nodes.
- **When** $\alpha \to \infty$: The penalty is so severe that the tree is pruned all the way down to a **single root node** (predicting the overall average $\bar{y}$ for everything).

::: {.callout-note title="Mathematical Intuition"}
As $\alpha$ increases from 0, subtrees are pruned in a deterministic nested sequence:

$$T_0 \supset T_1 \supset T_2 \supset \dots \supset T_{\text{root}}$$

This guarantees that for every value of $\alpha$, there exists a unique optimal subtree to evaluate.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Selecting the Optimal $\alpha$ via Cross-Validation

Because $\alpha$ is a hyperparameter, its optimal value cannot be determined from training data alone. We use $K$-Fold Cross-Validation:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Full Dataset] --> B[Grow a Large<br>Regression Tree T₀]
    B --> C[Generate Pruned Subtrees<br>for Different Cₚ Values]
    C --> D[10-Fold<br>Cross-Validation]
    D --> E[Compare Cross-Validated<br>Error: xerror]
    E --> F{Selection Rule}
    F --> G[Minimum-Error Tree]
    F --> H[1-SE Tree:<br>Simpler Tree Within 1 SE]
    G --> I[Prune T₀]
    H --> I
```

1.  **Cross-Validation Split:** Divide the training data into $K$ folds (e.g., $K = 10$).
2.  **Evaluate Subtrees:** For each candidate value of $\alpha$, fit the pruned tree on $K-1$ folds and compute the Cross-Validated Root Mean Squared Error ($\text{RMSE}_{\text{CV}}$) on the validation fold.
3.  **Pick** $\alpha$: Choose either:
    - **`select_best("rmse")`:** The $\alpha$ that achieves the absolute minimum cross-validated error.
    - **`select_by_one_std_err()` (1-SE Rule):** The simplest tree (highest $\alpha$) whose error is within one standard error of the minimum error. This favors parsimonious, highly interpretable models.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Step 1: Baseline Manual Trees (Fixed Hyperparameters)

```{r reg-tree-fit}
# 1. Fixed Model Specification
reg_tree_spec <- decision_tree(
  cost_complexity = 0.001, # typical range: 0.0001 to 0.1; fixed Cp; later replaced with tune()
  tree_depth = 8, # typical range: 2 to 10
  min_n = 25 # typical range: 10 to 100
) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("regression")

# 2. Workflow Setup
reg_tree_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(reg_rec) |>
  add_model(reg_tree_spec)

# 3. Fit Model
reg_tree_fit <- fit(reg_tree_wf, data = camp_train)

# 4. Evaluate on test set (predictions are on log scale — back-transform with exp)
reg_tree_preds <- augment(reg_tree_fit, new_data = camp_test) |>
  mutate(
    pred_dollar = exp(.pred), # back-transform to dollars
    actual_dollar = avg_order_amt # already in dollars (not log-transformed in test)
  )

# Baseline Performance Metrics
# we evaluate on the original scale for interpretability
baseline_tree_metrics <- reg_tree_preds |>
  summarise(
    rmse = sqrt(mean((pred_dollar - actual_dollar)^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
    mae = mean(abs(pred_dollar - actual_dollar), na.rm = TRUE),
    r2 = cor(pred_dollar, actual_dollar, use = "complete.obs")^2
  )

baseline_tree_metrics
```

```{r reg-tree-plot, fig.height=6, fig.width=10}
reg_tree_fit |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot(
    type = 4,
    extra = 1,
    main = "Regression Tree — Average Order Amount (log scale)",
    box.palette = "Blues"
  )
```

### Step 2: Automated Hyperparameter Tuning via 10-Fold Cross-Validation

Rather than guessing the best value for `cost_complexity` ($\alpha$ / $C_p$), we can mark it as `tune()` and use **10-Fold Cross-Validation** on the training set to find the optimal parameter value automatically.

```{r}
camp_train |>
  filter(is.na(log_avg_order_amt))
```

```{r}
# 1. Model Specification with Tuneable Cost-Complexity
tune_tree_spec <- decision_tree(
  cost_complexity = tune(), # tune Cp
  tree_depth = 8, # held fixed for comparison
  min_n = 25 # held fixed for comparison
) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("regression")

# 2. Workflow Setup
tune_tree_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(reg_rec) |>
  add_model(tune_tree_spec)

# 3. Create 10-Fold Cross-Validation Resamples
set.seed(2025)
folds <- vfold_cv(camp_train, v = 10)

# 4. Define Grid of Candidate Alpha (Cp) Values
cp_grid <- grid_regular(
  cost_complexity(range = c(-4, -1)), # Evaluates 10^-4 to 10^-1
  levels = 20 # 20 candidate values of Cp (alpha) to evaluate
)

# 5. Execute 10-Fold Cross-Validation
tune_results <- tune_grid(
  tune_tree_wf,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = cp_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq, mae),
  control = control_grid(verbose = FALSE, allow_par = TRUE) # allow parallel processing if a backend is registered
)

# 6. Plot the Pruning / Tuning Curve
autoplot(tune_results) +
  labs(
    title = "10-Fold Cross-Validation Tuning Curve",
    x = "Cost-Complexity Parameter (Alpha / Cp)",
    y = "Cross-Validated Performance Metric"
  )
```

::: {.callout-note title="Warning in Console Output"}
```         
- Warning(s) x10: A correlation computation is required, but `estimate` is constant and has 0 standard dev...
```

When cost_complexity is set too high, `rpart` prunes the tree down to a single root node that predicts a constant mean ($\bar{y}$). As a result, $R^2$ cannot compute a standard deviation and returns NA for extreme $C_p$ values.
:::

### Step 3: Selecting Best Hyperparameter & Finalizing the Model

We select the best `cost_complexity` value using the **1-Standard Error rule** (`select_by_one_std_err()`), which selects the simplest tree whose performance is within one standard error of the absolute minimum error.

```{r}
# 1. Select Best Cp using the 1-SE Rule

best_cp_1se <- select_by_one_std_err(
  tune_results,
  metric = "rmse",
  desc(cost_complexity) # prefer larger cp (simpler tree)
)

select_best(tune_results, metric = "rmse")

cat("Chosen Cost-Complexity (Cp):", best_cp_1se$cost_complexity, "\n")

# 2. Finalize Workflow with Tuned Cp
final_tree_wf <- finalize_workflow(tune_tree_wf, best_cp_1se)

# 3. Fit Final Pruned Model on Full Training Data
final_tree_fit <- fit(final_tree_wf, data = camp_train)

# 4. Evaluate Tuned Model on Test Set
final_tree_preds <- augment(final_tree_fit, new_data = camp_test) |>
  mutate(
    pred_dollar = exp(.pred),
    actual_dollar = avg_order_amt
  )

# Compare Metrics against Manual Baseline
tuned_tree_metrics <- final_tree_preds |>
  summarise(
    rmse = sqrt(mean((pred_dollar - actual_dollar)^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
    mae = mean(abs(pred_dollar - actual_dollar), na.rm = TRUE),
    r2 = cor(pred_dollar, actual_dollar, use = "complete.obs")^2
  )

baseline_tree_metrics |>
  mutate(model = "Baseline Tree Metrics") |>
  bind_rows(
    tuned_tree_metrics |>
      mutate(model = "Tuned Tree Metrics")
  ) |>
  relocate(model, .before = 1)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Why Did the 'Tuned' Model Have Worse Test Metrics?"}
Looking at the test set metrics, the baseline manual tree ($RMSE = 50.1$) appears to outperform the CV-tuned tree ($RMSE = 52.1$). Why did automated tuning give us a "worse" result?

1.  **Sampling Variation in the Test Set:** Cross-validation estimates performance across 10 different folds of the training data. The holdout test set is a single sample. By chance, the manual model's extra complexity happened to fit the test set's specific data points better.

2.  **The 1-SE Rule Favors Simplicity:** Using `select_by_one_std_err()` intentionally selects a simpler, more pruned tree to guard against overfitting. A simpler tree may yield slightly higher RMSE on a specific test set, but it produces a much cleaner, more robust flowchart for business decision-making.

3.  **Manual Guesses Can Be Lucky:** A manually chosen $C_p = 0.001$ happened to work well here, but without cross-validation, we would have no principled way of knowing whether that guess was safe or severely overfitted.
:::

### Visualizing the Final Tuned / Pruned Regression Tree

```{r}
# Visualize the Tuned / Pruned Tree
final_tree_fit |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot(
    type = 4, #split condition is shown beside each branch
    extra = 1, #displays the number of observations in the node
    main = "Regression Tree — Average Order Amount (CV Tuned)",
    box.palette = "Blues"
  )
```

### Printing out the Final Regression Tree and its Node Statistics

- The printout from below code chunk shows the final regression tree fit on the training data. It reports the number of observations in each node, the deviance (a measure of within-node variation), and the predicted value for `log(avg_order_amt)`.

- This print out should have the same informaton as the **visual tree diagram**, but it is often easier to read the exact numbers in this format.

```{r regression-tree-fit-engine}
final_tree_fit |>
  extract_fit_engine()
```

#### How to Interpret the Final Regression Tree

- For every node, rpart reports the `node number`, `splitting rule`, `number of observations`, `deviance`, and `fitted value`.

- 

  - denotes terminal node

- The columns mean:

- **node**: the node’s identification number

- split: the rule defining which observations enter that node

- n: the number of observations in that node

- **deviance**: the remaining within-node variation in the outcome

- **yval**: the node’s predicted outcome value ($\hat{y}$), which is the average of all observations in that node.

- **Node 1**

  ```         
  1) root 3053 616.7939000 4.552768  
  ```

  - **Node 1**: The root node contains all 3,053 observations in the training set.
  - The average predicted value for `log(avg_order_amt)` is $4.55$ (on the log scale: exp(4.55) = $94.63$).
  - The deviance of $616.79$ indicates the total variation in the outcome variable at this node.

::: callout-tip
- The regression tree was fitted after applying a natural-log transformation to `avg_order_amt`. Therefore, the yval displayed at each node is a prediction of `log(avg_order_amt)`, not a dollar amount.

- To express a terminal-node prediction on the original scale, apply the exponential function. For example, a terminal-node value of 4.214 corresponds to approximately `exp(4.214) = $67.62`.

- To make a prediction, begin at the root and follow the split conditions until reaching a node marked with an asterisk.

- Because categorical predictors were converted to one-hot dummy variables, conditions such as `device_desktop < 0.5` mean “not desktop,” while `device_desktop >= 0.5` means “desktop.”

- For integer count variables, a condition such as `cart_adds_30d < 1.5` means zero or one cart addition.
:::

### Terminal Nodes Statistics and Business Interpretation

```{r regression-tree-rules}
final_tree_fit |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot::rpart.rules(cover = TRUE, style = "tall", roundint = FALSE)
```

The final regression tree identifies **device type**, **loyalty tier**, and **acquisition channel** as the primary variables defining customer segments with different predicted average order amounts.

Because `avg_order_amt` was log-transformed before fitting the model, the terminal-node predictions are reported on the log scale. To return them approximately to the original dollar scale, apply the exponential function:

$$\widehat{\text{Order Amount}} =\exp\left(\widehat{\log(\text{Order Amount})}\right)$$
The approximate back-transformed predictions are:

| Log-scale prediction | Approximate order amount |
|---------------------:|-------------------------:|
|                  4.3 |                     \$74 |
|                  4.5 |                     \$90 |
|                  4.7 |                    \$110 |
|                  4.9 |                    \$134 |

::: {.callout-note title="Interpreting the Back-Transformed Predictions"}
Exponentiating a log-scale prediction returns an approximate typical order amount in dollars. Because of retransformation bias, it should not necessarily be interpreted as an unbiased estimate of the arithmetic mean order amount.
:::

#### 1. Desktop Customers Tend to Place Higher-Value Orders

The clearest overall pattern is the difference between desktop customers and mobile or tablet customers.

For Bronze and Silver loyalty members:

- Mobile or tablet users acquired through display, paid search, or social channels have a predicted order amount of approximately \$74.

- Desktop users acquired through display or social channels have a predicted order amount of approximately \$90.

- Desktop users acquired through direct, email, or paid search channels have a predicted order amount of approximately \$110.

The highest-value terminal node also consists of desktop users:

> **Desktop customers whose loyalty status is Gold, Platinum, new, or unknown have a predicted order amount of approximately \$134.**

**Business implication**: Desktop shopping may be associated with more deliberate or higher-value purchases. The company should investigate whether mobile customers experience checkout friction, weaker product presentation, or fewer opportunities for cross-selling and product bundling.

This finding is predictive rather than causal. It does not prove that moving a customer from mobile to desktop would increase spending. Device type may instead reflect purchase context, customer characteristics, or shopping intent.

#### 2. Loyalty Status Is Strongly Associated with Customer Value

Higher loyalty tiers are generally associated with larger predicted order amounts.

Among mobile or tablet customers acquired through direct or email channels:

- Bronze or Silver customers have a predicted order amount of approximately \$90.
- Gold, Platinum, new, or unknown customers have a predicted order amount of approximately \$110.

Among desktop customers, the Gold, Platinum, new, or unknown group forms the highest-value segment, with a predicted order amount of approximately \$134.

**Business implication**: Loyalty status appears useful for customer segmentation, personalization, and offer design. Higher-value loyalty segments may be appropriate targets for premium products, product bundles, early access, personalized recommendations, and retention campaigns.

::: {.callout-warning title="Investigate the New and Unknown Categories"}
The tree groups new and unknown loyalty statuses with Gold and Platinum customers. This does not necessarily mean that new or missing-tier customers behave like highly loyal customers in general. It means only that, within this branch of the tree, their observed order amounts were similar enough for the model to group them together.

These categories should be investigated separately before designing a marketing campaign.
:::

#### 3. Direct and Email Channels Are Associated with Higher Order Values

Direct and email traffic generally appears in higher-value terminal nodes than display or social traffic.

For mobile or tablet Bronze and Silver customers:

- Display, paid search, or social channels correspond to approximately \$74.
- Direct or email channels correspond to approximately \$90.

For desktop Bronze and Silver customers:

- Display or social channels correspond to approximately \$90.
- Direct, email, or paid search channels correspond to approximately \$110.

**Business implication**: Direct and email channels may attract customers with stronger purchase intent or an existing relationship with the brand. Email campaigns could emphasize higher-value products, bundles, replenishment reminders, loyalty benefits, and personalized recommendations.

This is also an associative finding. Direct traffic may represent customers who already know and trust the brand rather than proving that the direct channel itself causes higher spending.

#### 4. The Largest Low-Value Segment Represents an Important Opportunity

The largest terminal node covers approximately 25% of customers:

> Mobile or tablet users who are Bronze or Silver loyalty members and were acquired through display, paid search, or social channels have a predicted order amount of approximately \$74.

This is both the largest customer segment and the segment with the lowest predicted order amount.

**Business implication**: Because this segment contains approximately one-quarter of the observations, even a modest improvement in its average order value could produce a meaningful overall business impact.

Possible actions include:

- improving mobile landing pages and checkout usability;
- offering product bundles or quantity discounts;
- using free-shipping thresholds to encourage larger baskets;
- aligning advertising creative with higher-value products;
- retargeting customers who demonstrate stronger engagement; and
- encouraging loyalty-program enrollment or progression.

#### 5. High-Value Desktop Customers Are Smaller but Strategically Attractive

The highest-value terminal node covers approximately 8% of customers:

> **Desktop users whose loyalty status is Gold, Platinum, new, or unknown have a predicted order amount of approximately \$134.**

Although this segment is smaller than the broad mobile segments, its predicted order value is substantially higher.

**Business implication**: This group may justify more personalized treatment, including premium merchandising, VIP communications, exclusive offers, early product access, and higher allowable acquisition or retention costs.

#### 6. The Tree Reveals Interactions Rather Than Isolated Effects

The results should not be summarized simply as:

> Desktop is better.

or:

> Email is better.

The predicted order amount depends on combinations of customer characteristics.

For example, paid search appears in both:

- the lowest-value mobile or tablet Bronze and Silver segment; and
- the higher-value desktop Bronze and Silver segment.

Therefore, the relationship between paid search and order value depends on device type and loyalty status.

This is one of the main advantages of decision trees: they reveal conditional relationships and interactions that may be difficult to communicate through a single overall average or regression coefficient.

#### Overall Business Interpretation

> The regression tree identifies device type, loyalty tier, and acquisition channel as the primary dimensions of customer-value segmentation. Desktop customers generally have higher predicted order amounts than mobile or tablet customers, particularly among higher loyalty tiers. Direct and email traffic also tends to be associated with higher-value orders than display or social traffic.

The largest business opportunity appears to be the mobile or tablet Bronze and Silver segment acquired through display, paid search, or social channels. This group represents approximately one-quarter of customers but has the lowest predicted order amount. The company should investigate improvements to the mobile shopping experience, loyalty development, channel-specific merchandising, and basket-building strategies.

At the same time, the smaller high-value desktop segment may warrant premium retention and personalization efforts.

::: {.callout-important title="Important Limitations"}
These results describe predictive associations in the available data. They do not establish that device type, loyalty tier, or acquisition channel causes a change in average order amount.

Small segments, data-quality issues, and omitted variables should also be considered before making major business decisions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Reading the Coverage Percentages"}
The terminal-node coverage percentages add to approximately 99% rather than exactly 100% because `rpart.rules()` rounds the displayed percentages.
:::

#### Executive Interpretation of the Final Regression Tree

> **Tasks**: Identify three meaningful customer segments from the final regression tree. For each segment, describe the decision path, convert the terminal-node prediction to the original dollar scale, explain the possible business meaning, and recommend one practical action. Also note any limitations related to sample size, causality, or model uncertainty.

- **Device is the first and most important segmentation variable**. Desktop users generally have higher predicted order amounts than non-desktop users.

- **Email appears valuable in several branches.** For example, higher-income non-desktop email users with at least two cart additions have relatively high predicted order amounts.

- **Recent cart activity is a strong buying-intent signal.** Customers with at least two cart additions often receive higher predictions than otherwise similar customers with zero or one.

- **Loyalty status helps distinguish high-value segments.** Tier 4 customers tend to have higher predicted outcomes in the non-desktop email branch.

- **Some segments are small and should be treated cautiously.** The social-channel branch with fewer than two annual purchases contains only nine observations, so that result may be unstable.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Comparison: Classification Trees vs. Regression Trees

|  |  |  |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Feature** | **Classification Trees** | **Regression Trees** |
| **Target Variable (**$Y$) | Categorical (e.g., `Apparel`, `Electronics`) | Continuous (e.g., `Income`, `Orders`) |
| **Prediction at Leaf** | Majority Class Label (or Class Probabilities) | Sample Mean ($\bar{y}$) of observations in leaf |
| **Splitting Metric** | Gini Impurity ($G$) or Entropy | Residual Sum of Squares ($\text{RSS}$) |
| **Prediction Function** | Discrete regional boundary decisions | Piecewise constant step function |
| **Evaluation Metrics** | Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, ROC AUC | RMSE, MAE, $R^2$ |
| **Handling Outliers in** $Y$ | Robust (classes are counted, not averaged) | Sensitive (extreme $y$ values pull the leaf mean $\bar{y}$) |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 2: Ensembles {.unnumbered style="font-size: 28pt; font-weight: bold; color: #f1861b;"}

# **Random Forests**

## Conceptual Overview

A single decision tree is **high variance** — small changes in the training data can produce very different trees. The solution is **bagging (Bootstrap AGGregating)**:

1.  Draw $B$ bootstrap samples from the training data (sample with replacement)
2.  Fit a full decision tree on each bootstrap sample
3.  **Average** the predictions across all $B$ trees (regression) or **take a majority vote** (classification)

Averaging over many trees reduces variance dramatically while keeping bias roughly the same — the key insight behind ensemble methods.

::: {.callout-note title="Bagging alone is not enough — feature randomness"}
If all predictors are strong, every bagged tree will tend to use the same top predictors at its first split. The resulting trees are **highly correlated** — averaging correlated predictions doesn't reduce variance as much as averaging independent predictions.

**Random forests** fix this with **feature randomness**: at each split, only a random subset of $m$ predictors is considered (controlled by `mtry`). This forces trees to use different predictors, de-correlating them and producing larger variance reduction when averaged.

Typical default: $m = \sqrt{p}$ for classification, $m = p/3$ for regression.
:::

### How Rows and Trees Relate in a Random Forest

Think of your dataset as a large spreadsheet:

- **Rows (**$N$): Individual observations in your training dataset (e.g., $N = 3,200$ customers).

- **Columns (**$p$): Features/predictors describing each row (e.g., `age`, `income`, `recency`).

- **Trees (**$B$): Complete, individual decision trees built inside the forest (e.g., $B = 500$ trees).

When you build a Random Forest with 500 trees (`trees = 500`), you are **not** matching 1 row to 1 tree. Instead, every single tree is trained on roughly $N$ rows sampled from your dataset:

```         
Full Dataset (e.g., 1,000 rows)
                                          │
            ┌─────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┐
            ▼                             ▼                             ▼
    Bootstrap Sample 1            Bootstrap Sample 2            Bootstrap Sample 500
   (~1,000 rows, sampled         (~1,000 rows, sampled         (~1,000 rows, sampled
     with replacement)             with replacement)             with replacement)
            │                             │                             │
            ▼                             ▼                             ▼
        [ Tree 1 ]                    [ Tree 2 ]                   [ Tree 500 ]
  (Full decision flowchart)     (Full decision flowchart)     (Full decision flowchart)
```

### From One Tree to Many: Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating)

A single decision tree is notorious for having **high variance**: small perturbations in the training data can alter the root split and result in a completely different tree structure.

To overcome this instability, we turn to an ensemble method called **Bagging (Bootstrap AGGregating)**:

1.  **Bootstrap Sampling:** Draw $B$ independent bootstrap samples from the training dataset (sampling $N$ observations *with replacement*).

2.  **Parallel Fitting:** Fit an unpruned, deep decision tree to each bootstrap sample.

3.  **Aggregating Predictions:** Combine the predictions across all $B$ trees:

    - **Regression:** Compute the average prediction: $\hat{f}_{\text{bag}}(x) = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B \hat{f}^b(x)$

      - $x$ = Input feature vector: e.g., a set of customer characteristics
      - $\hat{f}^b(x)$ = Prediction of Tree *b*
      - $\hat{f}_{\text{bag}}(x)$ = Final Bagged Estimate, which is the aggregated, overall ensemble prediction for observation $x$.

    - **Classification:** Take the majority vote (or average predicted class probabilities).

::: {.callout-note title="Regression vs. Classification"}
- For Regression (what this formula shows): The final prediction $\hat{f}_{\text{bag}}(x)$ is the continuous average of all $B$ numeric outputs.

- For Classification: Rather than averaging continuous values, each tree votes for a discrete class label, and $\hat{f}_{\text{bag}}(x)$ represents the majority vote (or the average predicted probability across all $B$ trees).
:::

#### Why Bagging Works: The Mathematics of Variance Reduction

If we have $B$ independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables each with variance $\sigma^2$, the variance of their average is:

$$\text{Var}\left(\frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B X_b\right) = \frac{\sigma^2}{B}$$

- $B$: The total number of trees in your ensemble (e.g., $B = 500$).

- $b$: The index for a specific tree, where $b = 1, 2, \dots, B$.

- $X_b$: The output/prediction of tree $b$ for a given observation $x$ (often written as $\hat{f}^b(x)$ in textbook notation).

- $\frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B X_b$: The average prediction across all $B$ trees in the ensemble (the Bagged / Random Forest estimate).

- $\sigma^2$: The variance of a single individual decision tree ($\text{Var}(X_b) = \sigma^2$).

As $B$ grows large, variance approaches zero. However, because bagged trees are trained on overlapping bootstrap samples from the same dataset, they are **correlated** (with pair-wise correlation $\rho > 0$). The true variance of an ensemble average is:

$$\text{Var}(\text{Ensemble}) = \rho \sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B} \sigma^2$$

As $B \to \infty$, the second term drops to zero, but the first term ($\rho \sigma^2$) remains. **If trees are highly correlated (**$\rho$ is large), bagging offers limited variance reduction.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### De-Correlating Trees: The Random Forest Breakthrough

If a dataset has one or two dominant predictors (e.g., `income` or `recency_days`), **every single bagged tree will select that dominant predictor for its root split**. Consequently, all trees in the bagged ensemble look almost identical ($\rho \approx 1$).

**Random Forests** fix this bottleneck by adding **feature randomness (sub-space sampling)** at every split:

::: {.callout-note title="The Key Difference: Split-Level Feature Subsampling"}
When building each tree, at **every individual split**, the algorithm randomly draws a candidate subset of $m$ features from the total $p$ available features ($m < p$). The tree is forced to choose the best split **only among those** $m$ candidates.

- **Classification Default:** $m = \sqrt{p}$
- **Regression Default:** $m = p/3$

By forcing trees to ignore dominant predictors at many nodes, feature randomness **decorrelates the trees** (lowers $\rho$), unlocking massive variance reduction when averaged.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Out-of-Bag (OOB) Error: "Free" Validation

Because each bootstrap sample selects approximately $63.2\%$ of unique observations, the remaining $\sim 36.8\%$ of data points are left out for that specific tree. These are called **Out-of-Bag (OOB)** observations.

``` r
Full Dataset (N) ──► [ Bootstrap Sample (~63.2%) ] ──► Train Tree b 
                └──► [ Out-of-Bag (OOB) (~36.8%) ] ──► Validate Tree b
```

- For each observation $i$, we can predict its value using **only the trees where observation** $i$ was OOB.
- Averaging these predictions yields the **OOB Error Rate**, which serves as an unbiased estimate of test error **without needing** $K$-fold cross-validation or a separate validation split.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Key Hyperparameters in `tidymodels` (`rand_forest`)

| Math Symbol | Concept | `tidymodels` Argument | Default (`ranger` engine) | Practical Guidance |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| $m$ | Candidate features per split | `mtry` | $\sqrt{p}$ (Class) / $p/3$ (Reg) | Primary tuning parameter. Smaller $m \to$ less tree correlation. |
| $B$ | Number of trees | `trees` | $500$ | More is generally better (does not overfit); set high enough for error to stabilize (e.g., $500–1000$). |
| $n_{\text{min}}$ | Min node size for split | `min_n` | $1$ (Class) / $5$ (Reg) | Controls tree depth/growth stopping. Lower values $\to$ deeper trees. |

### Feature Importance: Peeking Inside the "Black Box"

While individual decision trees produce simple flowchart diagrams, Random Forests aggregate hundreds of trees, sacrificing direct diagram visualizability. To restore interpretability, we measure **Variable Importance**:

1.  **Mean Decrease in Impurity (MDI / Gini Importance):** Sums the total reduction in Gini impurity (or RSS) brought about by splits on feature $X_j$, averaged across all trees.

2.  **Permutation Importance (OOB Drop):** Randomly shuffles (scrambles) feature $X_j$ in the OOB data and measures how much predictive accuracy degrades. Larger drops in accuracy indicate higher feature importance.

We can also use SHAP Values (Shapley Additive exPlanations) to quantify each feature's contribution to individual predictions; A brief introduction to SHAP is provided towards the end of the codebook (@sec-explaining-models).

## Random Forest with 10 Fold CV

### Fitting a Random Forest

::: callout-tip
This code chunk takes a long time to run due to computational complexity. Thus, we recommend running this using parallel processing.
:::

```{r rf-fit}
# 1. Parallel processing
library(doParallel)
cl <- makePSOCKcluster(parallel::detectCores() - 1)
registerDoParallel(cl)

# 2. Random Forest Model Specification
rf_spec <- rand_forest(
  trees = 500, # number of trees — more is generally better (diminishing returns)
  mtry = tune(), # number of predictors considered at each split
  min_n = tune() # minimum node size
) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "permutation") |> # enables variable importance
  set_mode("classification")

# 3. Workflow Setup
rf_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(class_rec) |>
  add_model(rf_spec)

# 4. Turning Grid: small grid for demonstration
set.seed(2025)
rf_grid <- grid_regular(
  mtry(range = c(3, 10)),
  min_n(range = c(5, 30)),
  levels = 3 #3 evenly spaced values for the two hyperparameters, leading to 3 x 3 = 9 total combinations
)

# 5. Tune Grid
rf_tune_results <- tune_grid(
  rf_wf,
  resamples = camp_folds, # 10-fold CV x 9 hyperparameter combinations = 90 total tree models
  grid = rf_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy)
)

# 6. Safely Close Cluster
stopImplicitCluster()
stopCluster(cl)

# 7 Plot Results
autoplot(rf_tune_results) +
  labs(title = "Random Forest Tuning — AUC Across mtry and min_n") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r rf-best}
best_rf <- select_best(rf_tune_results, metric = "roc_auc")
best_rf

final_rf_wf <- finalize_workflow(rf_wf, best_rf)
final_rf_fit <- fit(final_rf_wf, data = camp_train)
```

### Random Forest Performance

```{r rf-metrics}
rf_preds <- augment(final_rf_fit, new_data = camp_test)

rf_preds |>
  metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc, sens, spec)(
    truth = purchased,
    estimate = .pred_class,
    .pred_yes
  )
```

### The Effect of `mtry` — Feature Randomness

```{r mtry-effect}
# Show how AUC changes with mtry at the best min_n
rf_tune_results |>
  collect_metrics() |>
  filter(.metric == "roc_auc") |>
  group_by(mtry, min_n) |>
  summarise(mean_auc = round(mean(mean), 4), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(mean_auc))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Interpreting mtry"}
- A small `mtry` forces each tree to consider fewer predictors — trees become more diverse (less correlated) but individually weaker.

- A large `mtry` approaches *bagging* (all predictors available at each split) — trees are stronger individually but more correlated with each other.

The optimal `mtry` balances individual tree quality against ensemble diversity. With \~15 predictors in this dataset, `mtry` values between **3 and 8** typically work best.
:::

### Out-of-Bag (OOB) Error

```{r oob-error}
# ranger computes OOB error automatically during training
# Extract it from the fitted engine
oob_error <- final_rf_fit |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  _$prediction.error

cat("OOB error (misclassification rate):", round(oob_error, 4), "\n")
cat("OOB accuracy                       :", round(1 - oob_error, 4), "\n")

# Compare to CV accuracy
rf_tune_results |>
  collect_metrics() |>
  filter(.metric == "accuracy") |>
  summarise(cv_accuracy = round(mean(mean), 4))
```

::: {.callout-note title="What is OOB error?"}
- Each bootstrap sample in a random forest leaves out approximately **37% of the training observations** (observations not selected in that particular sample).

- These *out-of-bag* observations can be used to evaluate each tree without a separate validation set — the OOB error is essentially a free cross-validation estimate computed during training.

- OOB error tends to be slightly pessimistic compared to CV (because each tree only uses \~63% of the data) but is remarkably accurate and much faster to compute.

- \*\* For large forests and large datasets, OOB can replace CV entirely\*\*.
:::

### Variable Importance

```{r vip-rf, fig.height=6}
final_rf_fit |>
  extract_fit_parsnip() |>
  vip(
    num_features = 15,
    aesthetics = list(fill = "#154734", color = "white", alpha = 0.85)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Random Forest — Permutation Variable Importance",
    subtitle = "How much does prediction accuracy drop when each variable is randomly shuffled?"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Permutation importance vs. impurity importance"}
The `ranger` engine supports two importance measures:

**Impurity importance** (Gini-based): measures how much each variable decreases weighted Gini impurity across all splits in the forest. Fast to compute but tends to **favor variables with many unique values** (continuous variables and high-cardinality factors) — even if those variables aren't truly important predictors.

**Permutation importance** (what we use here): for each variable, randomly shuffle its values across all test observations and measure how much prediction accuracy drops. A variable that is truly important will cause a large accuracy drop when shuffled; a noise variable will cause little change. This is more reliable but slower to compute.

- We use `importance = "permutation"` in the engine call for this reason — it gives a fairer comparison across predictors with different scales and cardinalities.
:::

**Interpretation of Variable Importance**: The variable importance plot shows which features are most influential in the Random Forest's predictions. The higher the importance score, the more critical that feature is for accurate predictions.

- For example, knowing `cart_adds_30` is the #1 most important feature tells us it strongly impacts predictions, but it doesn't show whether Gold status increases or decreases the likelihood of purchase. Pair this with **SHAP** or **partial dependence plots** to explain the direction of the effect.

### Model Comparison: Single Tree vs. Random Forest on Prediction Performance

| Metric | Single Decision Tree | Random Forest Ensemble Tuned with 10F CV | Improvement |
|------------------|------------------|-------------------|------------------|
| **Accuracy** | 0.774 | **0.805** | +4.4% |
| **ROC AUC** | 0.761 | **0.799** | +5.8% |

::: {.callout-tip title="Why Random Forest is Superior?"}
By combining 500 decorrelated trees via **bagging** and **feature randomness (`mtry`)**, the Random Forest successfully reduced model variance, yielding a significantly higher ROC AUC on holdout test data compared to any individual decision tree.
:::

### Cost of Random Forest

- **Why use 10-Fold CV?** It fits into the standard `tidymodels` workflow (`tune_grid()`), making it easy to tune hyperparameters using the exact same code structure as Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, or XGBoost.

- **Alternative?** For massive datasets where running 10-Fold CV across a hyperparameter grid takes hours (or days), you can skip $K$-fold CV entirely. You can evaluate candidate models using their built-in **OOB Error**, which requires fitting each candidate forest **only once** instead of 10 times!

::: {.callout-tip title="Summary"}
- In the previous code, 10-Fold CV was used to search for the best combinations of `mtry` and `min_n` (3 x 3 = 9), leading to 90 forests.

- On the other hand, **OOB error** was calculated inside the single winning forest as a fast, built-in validation check.

- Both give nearly identical estimates of performance, but OOB requires a fraction of the computing power!
:::

## Random Forest with OBB Error

::: {.callout-tip title="Why OOB Tuning is Faster"}
- Instead of re-fitting each forest 10 times across 10 folds, you evaluate each candidate forest exactly ONCE on its own built-in Out-of-Bag (OOB) predictions.

- Because OOB estimation calculates out-of-sample error during training for free, you get 10x speedups (or more) while still finding optimal hyperparameters.

``` r
Standard 10-Fold CV Search:
Grid Choice 1 ──► [Fit Fold 1] [Fit Fold 2] ... [Fit Fold 10]  (10 Forests fit)
Grid Choice 2 ──► [Fit Fold 1] [Fit Fold 2] ... [Fit Fold 10]  (10 Forests fit)
...

OOB Validation Search:
Grid Choice 1 ──► [Fit 1 Forest on Full Train Data] ──► Extract OOB Error  (1 Forest fit)
Grid Choice 2 ──► [Fit 1 Forest on Full Train Data] ──► Extract OOB Error  (1 Forest fit)
```
:::

If you evaluate 20 grid settings:

- **10-Fold CV:** Fits $20 \times 10 = \mathbf{200\text{ forests}}$.

- **OOB Search:** Fits $20 \times 1 = \mathbf{20\text{ forests}}$ (**90% time reduction**).

### Method 1: Using Custom Engine-Level OOB Evaluation Loop

> To implement OOB tuning, we can create a custom loop that fits a Random Forest for each combination of hyperparameters in our grid and extracts the OOB error directly from the fitted model.
